prize_parts.citation: for design-based evidence on how technology and import competition reshape labour demand, local labour markets and wage inequality

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged: B030, credited to Autor, Hanson and Dorn. The chair asks for one test applied to every candidate: did the work change what can credibly be known, and has it been validated in use or in evidence? B030 passes on both. Newly assembled data and exposure-based quasi-experimental designs showed that import competition and technological change produce persistent, uneven local labour-market adjustment, not frictionless reallocation. The task framework gave a testable account of polarisation. Other authors have replicated and extended the core finding with other designs, datasets and countries, and the live debate is about magnitudes and persistence. It also answers a substantive question about who bears the costs of technological and trade change, which is a large, hard question with real consequences for research and policy. Round 1 changed one thing. I have narrowed the citation to the empirical labour-demand evidence and no longer claim the whole task framework, because credit for that extends to Levy, Murnane, Katz and Acemoglu, who are outside the credited set. I also now accept Dorn over Katz more firmly. Boppart has moved to the same view, and the Autor-Dorn-Hanson design is the identifiable joint contribution. On the common test, B005 is at least as mature and has a cleaner attribution core. I still put B030 first because I weigh a substantive, design-based finding about distributional consequences slightly above a measurement toolkit. That is a close judgement, and my labour-economics background may bias it.
statement.case_against: Maturity is lower than for B005, B014 or B027. The persistence and magnitude of the China-shock effects, and the shift-share identification behind them, are still debated. Credit for the technology strand is diffuse and includes people outside the set, among them an existing laureate. The technology and trade strands may be two achievements, not one, and a single citation could blur them. Adjacency to the 2023 and 2024 prizes may reduce marginal novelty. I draw the link between Katz's skill-bias work and the 2023 prize from general knowledge, not from the supplied evidence, and I have not verified it. The three-name cap excludes Katz. If the committee thinks the strands do not cohere, the China-shock work alone is the better-attributed piece, but that is a weaker prize than the one I propose.

responses.point: Strömberg ranks B030 sixth. He rates the China-shock evidence as strong but only moderately mature. He worries that combining trade and technology strands blurs the motivation, and he notes that Katz's skill-premium role is left out.
responses.response: The maturity concern is fair, and it is the main reason B030 is not an easy first choice. I would separate the existence of persistent local adjustment costs from their size. The first has held up across designs, and debate has moved to the second. On blurring, I would keep one citation about how external shocks to labour demand, trade and technology alike, translate into local labour-market outcomes. Autor works on both strands, and Dorn and Hanson are core to the trade-shock design. I would not add Katz's skill-premium strand, since that would widen the citation and invite the very blurring he describes. If colleagues judge the two strands incompatible in one prize, I would concede that B030 is weaker than I have presented it.

responses.point: Friberg ranks B005 first on breadth of use across merger review, antitrust, trade, health and environmental analysis, and has moved his third name from Bresnahan to Levinsohn. He acknowledges the reservation that it is a methods prize.
responses.response: Breadth of validated use is a legitimate common test, and B005 does very well on it. I also agree with his revised credit set, since a demand-estimation citation should name all three authors of the paper it rests on. My difference is about weighting. Breadth of use measures how many questions a tool serves. It does not by itself say how much the tool taught us about the economy. I give extra weight to work that combines new evidence with a framework that explains it, which is why I rank B030 first. I do not treat the methods label as disqualifying, and I regard B005 as the strongest alternative to my own choice. I would not oppose it if the committee weighs breadth of use and clean attribution more heavily than I do.

responses.point: Boppart keeps B030 as an alternative and has revised his third name from Katz to Dorn if B030 is pursued. He notes that the size and persistence of the trade-shock effects are still debated, and that the task framework owes much to people outside the credited set.
responses.response: I welcome the convergence on Dorn, since it removes the main attribution difference between us on B030. I agree that the task framework owes much to others, and my narrowed citation reflects that. I would apply the same discipline to every candidate. A citation should name only what the credited trio demonstrably did. Boppart's own B027 case does that well, because it states plainly that the mechanism's empirical validation is indirect. I accept the same candour for B030 on persistence and magnitude. Where I would disagree is in treating that debate as a reason to defer. Two decades of scrutiny is enough to judge influence even if the exact magnitudes are unsettled.

responses.point: Fredriksson ranks B030 seventh. He regards it as only moderately mature, with the long-run interpretation of the China shock and the shift-share methodology still debated, and he notes shared credit with Katz, Acemoglu and others.
responses.response: His maturity point is the strongest objection to B030, and I do not dismiss it. I agree that B030 is less mature than B014 or B005. I weigh the identification standard differently from him. B030 rests on design-based variation, whereas he himself concedes that B014's constitutional evidence is largely cross-country and observational. I also think the credit problem is smaller for the China-shock strand than for the task framework, so a narrowly worded citation avoids most of it. I would not say B030 is more mature than B014, only that its evidence is cleaner on identification. Whether that offsets lower maturity is a judgement on which reasonable members can differ.

uncertainties: Whether the persistence and magnitude debate on China-shock effects, and shift-share identification, should be read as limiting maturity or as normal refinement of a replicated finding.
Whether the technology (task) and trade-shock strands form one coherent prize motivation or two separate achievements, and whether the China-shock work alone would be the better-attributed prize.
Whether Dorn or Katz is the better third name. I now lean firmly to Dorn, but my view of Katz's overlap with prior recognition draws on general knowledge that I have not verified.
How the committee should weigh a methods and measurement contribution (B005) against a substantive, design-based finding (B030). I have no agreed way to compare them, and my own field may bias me.
Whether adjacency to the 2023 and 2024 prizes should count as a bar or only as a weight against marginal contribution. I treat it as a weight, and I have not verified the claims about prior prizes.
statement.conflict_note: No co-authorship or institutional tie to Autor, Hanson, Dorn or any other credited name on the shortlist appears in my supplied profile. My frequent co-authors (Bayer, Anwar, Lindquist, Holmlund, Lochner, Bindler) are not on the shortlist. I work in labour economics and the economics of crime, which is field proximity to B030, B001 and B009, and I disclose it without adjudicating it. I presented the 2023 prize (Goldin) at the announcement, and I note the topical adjacency to B030. Presentation speeches may reflect collective drafting, and I do not treat that role as evidence of a preference or as a conflict. I have no other updates to my round 1 disclosure.
